title: Lee Takes the Blame at Gettysburg
text:
On July 3, 1863, the third day of the Battle of Gettysburg, General Robert E. Lee ordered a massive frontal assault on the center of the Union line. About twelve thousand Confederate soldiers, in what became known as Pickett's Charge, marched across nearly a mile of open fields under artillery and rifle fire. The attack failed, and about half of them were killed, wounded or captured.

Arthur Fremantle, a British army officer who was traveling with the Confederate army as an observer, watched what happened next and recorded it in his account published that same year. Lee rode out alone to meet the shattered troops as they streamed back, encouraging them and telling them to rally. When a distraught brigade commander, Cadmus Wilcox, came up to report the state of his men, Fremantle heard Lee tell him not to mind: all this had been his own fault, it was he who had lost the fight, and Wilcox must help him out of it as best he could.

The army retreated to Virginia. In August, Lee wrote to Jefferson Davis offering to resign his command. Davis refused, and Lee led the army until the end of the war.
lesson: When a decision you made fails, say so plainly and first. Taking the blame yourself keeps your people's trust when it is most fragile.
people: Robert E. Lee, Arthur Fremantle, Cadmus Wilcox
source: Arthur J. L. Fremantle, Three Months in the Southern States (1863); Lee's letter to Jefferson Davis, August 8, 1863
